categories.name: Seasonal flowers
categories.description: What the market is bringing, what is about to peak and what we are arranging with it: notes on the flowers of each season, from the first plum to the last chrysanthemum.

tags.name: Autumn
tags.description: Maple, chrysanthemum, persimmon branches and the last grasses: notes from September to early December.

posts.title: The autumn term opens, with two new evening classes
posts.excerpt: Twelve weeks of maple and chrysanthemum, a new Friday evening class for beginners and a few trial seats on Wednesdays.
posts.content:
The autumn term starts on Tuesday 6 October and runs to the week before Christmas. The flowers change almost weekly from now on: maple while it is still green at the edges, then the first chrysanthemums, persimmon branches with the fruit left on, and at the very end of the term, the bare willow we use for the new-year lesson.

Two classes are new this term. A First Branch class on Friday evenings at seven, for people who could never make the daytime one, and an after-work class on Wednesdays at half past six that keeps two seats each week for trial lessons.

Seats this term

  • First Branch, Tuesday 10:00 — two seats
  • First Branch, Friday 19:00 — four seats
  • Seasonal Line, Tuesday 19:00 — full, waiting list open
  • Trial lessons — Saturdays at 10:00 and Wednesdays at 18:30

Autumn is the easiest season to begin. Everything is already leaning.

Ren Takagi

You can join at any point in the term; the fee is counted from your first lesson.

posts.title: Choosing your first pin frog
posts.excerpt: Round or oblong, heavy or light, brass pins or steel: what to look for in a kenzan, and why we lend ours for the whole first term.
posts.content:
The pin frog, kenzan, is the heavy disc of upright needles that holds every stem in a shallow basin. It is the one tool you will use in every lesson, and the one most people buy wrongly at first.

What to look for

  • Weight. Heavier is better; a light one tips as soon as a branch leans.
  • Size. A round one about seven centimetres across fits most basins.
  • Pins. Close together, upright and not too sharp at the tips.

We lend a pin frog and scissors to every student for the first term, so there is no need to buy anything before you know you will stay. When you do, we can order a set for you at cost.

posts.title: The students' exhibition, 24 to 26 October
posts.excerpt: Forty arrangements, three days, two doors from the studio. Free entry, and tea on the Saturday afternoon.
posts.content:
Our thirty-seventh students' exhibition opens on Saturday 24 October in the small gallery by the canal, two doors from the studio. Every student who wants to shows one piece: first-term beginners next to this year's certificate class.

The flowers are bought on the Thursday and the arrangements are finished on the Friday evening. By Sunday afternoon they are already changing, which is rather the point of showing them.

An exhibition of ikebana is an exhibition of three days. That is what makes it worth the walk.

Sayo Mizuhara

Open 10:00 to 17:00, last day until 15:00. Free entry. Tea and sweets on the Saturday from two.

posts.title: Grasses at the end of summer
posts.excerpt: Clear glass, cold water and a handful of grasses: the arrangement we teach in the last week before the August break.
posts.content:
In the heat of late summer we put the basins away and bring out the glass. Water you can see becomes part of the arrangement, and grasses are the best thing to put in it: thin, moving, and almost free.

The trick is to let the stems cross inside the glass, so they hold each other up. Change the water every day and cut a centimetre off the stems each time; they will last a week.

posts.title: Why the shortest line matters
posts.excerpt: Beginners fuss over the tall line. The arrangement is usually saved, or lost, by the short one at the bottom.
posts.content:
Every new student spends the first lessons on shin, the tall line: the right branch, the right height, the right lean. It matters. But when an arrangement looks wrong and nobody can say why, the answer is nearly always hikae, the short line low on the other side.

Hikae is what closes the triangle. Without it the tall line floats, and the whole arrangement seems about to tip over. With it too long, the triangle becomes a fan and the space between the lines disappears.

Look at the short line first. The tall one will tell you if it is unhappy.

Yui Asami

posts.title: Iris in a shallow basin
posts.excerpt: Iris grows at the water's edge, so we arrange it the same way: leaves in groups, flowers low, and plenty of open water.
posts.content:
Early June is iris season, and the iris is the one flower we always arrange as if it were still growing. The leaves go in first, in groups of three, the way they come out of the ground; the flowers sit lower than you expect; and a third of the basin is left as open water.

The leaves are the difficult part. Each one has a front and a back, and they must all face the same way, so you will spend some time turning them over. That is normal.

posts.title: A morning with the cherry branches
posts.excerpt: Cherry is the hardest branch of the year to arrange: everyone loves it, so everyone puts in too much.
posts.content:
For two weeks in spring every class asks for cherry. We buy it in bud, keep it in a cold room, and bring it out the morning before the lesson so it opens on the table.

The rule we give: choose one branch, then put half of it back. The blossom is so full that a single line does the work of three, and the empty space around it is what makes it look like spring and not like a shop window.

posts.title: Pine, bamboo and plum for the new year
posts.excerpt: The new-year arrangement, step by step: the three friends of winter in one tall vase, and how to keep them for two weeks.
posts.content:
Pine for long life, bamboo for strength, plum because it flowers in the snow: the three friends of winter have been arranged together at the new year for centuries, and every January the first lesson is theirs.

Pine lasts for weeks if you spray the needles; the plum opens slowly in a warm room. Cut the bamboo just above a joint and fill it with water, and it will stay green until the plum is over.
